title: Body Temperature

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Your body is really two temperatures at once. Deep inside, where the brain, heart, lungs, and gut live, the temperature barely budges, because your body spends real energy defending it. Out at the skin, the temperature drifts with whatever is going on around you, warm in a hot shower, cold on a windy walk. 'Core' means that stable inner number, and it is the one that tells you whether a person is actually sick. So a patient with icy hands is not hypothermic just because their hands are cold, and a thermometer placed nearer the middle gets closer to the truth than one touching the outside.

### Question 2

Everyone's temperature drifts around a bit during a normal day, so a useful cutoff has to sit high enough that ordinary drifting will not cross it by accident. Public health agencies picked 100.4°F, which is exactly 38.0°C. That is why the Fahrenheit number looks so oddly specific: the round number is the Celsius one, and the Fahrenheit value is just the conversion. Also worth knowing, CDC's screening definition does not require a thermometer at all. Feeling hot to the touch or reporting that you have felt feverish also counts, which matters when someone has already taken acetaminophen and knocked the reading down.

### Question 3

A wall thermostat does not produce a single unit of heat. All it does is know the target number, read the current number, and flip switches. The hypothalamus plays exactly that role. The switches it flips are your sweat glands, the blood vessels in your skin, your shivering muscles, and hormones that speed up metabolism. So when you see a question about something that makes heat, like thyroid hormone or muscle, that is an effector, the furnace. The controller is the part doing the comparing, and that is the hypothalamus.

### Question 4

Picture the thermostat sitting at 70 and someone quietly moving it to 78. The room has not changed, but relative to the new target it is now eight degrees too cold, so the furnace kicks on hard. Nothing is malfunctioning. Fever chemicals move your body's target the same way, so your muscles start their shivering furnace and your skin blood vessels clamp shut to keep heat in. The patient feels freezing and piles on blankets while the number on the thermometer is climbing, and both things are true at once.

### Question 5

The difference is not how hot the person is, it is whether the system is following orders or has been overrun. In fever, the body chose a higher target and is deliberately working toward it, which is why the patient shivers on the way up. In hyperthermia, nobody changed the target. A person is locked in a hot car, or running a marathon in August, or reacting to anesthesia, and heat simply piles in faster than sweat and blood flow can carry it out. Because fever medicine works by moving the target, it accomplishes nothing when the target was never moved. That case needs ice, water, shade, and speed.

### Question 6

Test yourself with hot soup. Rest the spoon against your lip and heat moves by touching, that is conduction. Now hold your palm out to the side of the bowl, level with it and out of the rising steam, and you still feel a faint warmth crossing the gap. Nothing is touching you and no air is blowing on you, because that heat is crossing the space as invisible infrared light, the same way a campfire warms your face from several feet away, that is radiation. Blow across the surface and the soup cools faster because you swept off the hot layer of air sitting on top and replaced it with cool air, that is convection. Watch out for one trap: the warmth you feel directly above the bowl is mostly hot air and steam rising into your hand, so that one is convection, not radiation. Leave the bowl sitting out and it slowly steams away and cools, that is evaporation. A fan works by convection, which is exactly why a fan feels useless in a room that is already hotter than you are: it is now sweeping hot air onto you instead of away.

### Question 7

Your temperature is not a flat line, it is a slow wave riding an internal 24-hour clock. It bottoms out in the small hours while you are deep asleep and crests in the late afternoon and early evening. The wave is driven by the clock itself, not just by whether you have been moving around, which is why night shift workers still show it. Two practical consequences: patients and families often notice fevers 'spiking at night' when part of that is the normal wave stacking on top of the illness, and a single number means little unless you know what time it was taken. That is why the time gets charted alongside the value.

### Question 8

Two thermometers reading differently does not automatically mean one is broken. Under the tongue sits in a pocket fed by deep blood supply; under the arm sits out at the edge of the body where skin, sweat, and room air all get a vote. The arm is going to read lower, reliably, by about a degree Fahrenheit. The trap is trending. If yesterday's chart says axillary and today someone takes an oral reading, the number jumps a degree and it looks like the patient changed when only the location did. Pick a site, stay with it, and always write down which one you used.

### Question 9

Adults warm up by shivering, which is muscle doing rapid useless work purely to waste energy as heat. Newborns cannot do that well yet, so they arrive with a specialized fuel, brown fat, that they burn directly for warmth. The catch is the bill: burning it consumes oxygen and glucose fast, so a cold newborn can slide into low blood sugar and breathing trouble surprisingly quickly. Notice also the distinction the wrong answers lean on. Clamping down skin blood vessels keeps heat in, it does not make heat. That is why the delivery room response is not just a blanket but drying first, since a wet baby loses heat by evaporation faster than any blanket can compensate.

### Question 10

Fever is the body ringing an alarm bell, and in an older adult the bell is both quieter and starts from a lower resting pitch. Someone whose usual temperature is 97.2 sitting at 99.1 has moved almost two degrees, which is a real signal even though the number never crosses the familiar 100.4 line. This is why infection specialists set lower cutoffs for nursing home residents specifically, and why more than half of long-term care residents with serious infection never meet the classic fever definition at all. The practical habit is to know the person's own baseline and to weigh the non-temperature clues, because in this population sudden confusion is often the loudest sign of infection.

### Question 11

The chill phase and the flush phase are the same mismatch running in opposite directions. On the way up, the target moved above the body and the body chased it, so the patient shivered under blankets. On the way down, the target drops back to normal while the body is still hot, so now the body is above target and dumps heat as fast as it can: skin vessels open wide, giving the flushed red look, and sweat pours out to carry heat away as it evaporates. The order matters and is worth getting straight. The set point moves first and the temperature follows, never the reverse. All that sweat is water leaving the body, so this is the moment to think about fluids.

### Question 12

Think about which lever each option pulls. The antipyretic pulls the target back down, and once the target is down the body cools itself for free using the tools it already has. The sponge bath does not touch the target at all; it just hauls heat off the skin while the hypothalamus is still insisting the body should be hot. The hypothalamus notices and pushes back with shivering, which burns oxygen and makes the patient miserable, and sometimes leaves them no cooler than before. The exception is the situation where there is no raised target to reset, like heat stroke. There, physical cooling is the whole treatment and fever medicine is beside the point.
